newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Lindsey sees more small-loan securitization.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Lindsey sees more small-loan securitization.

text.p: Banks will be able to package small business loans into securities more easily in future as better methods are developed for assessing risk, Federal Reserve Governor Lawrence Lindsey said Wednesday.

Speaking to a small business conference sponsored by the Richmond regional Fed bank, Lindsey said the ability to "securitize" smaller loans should mean lower costs and greater liquidity for small business owners.

"Clearly not all small business loans are going to be appropriate candidates for securitization, and not all banks will wish to adopt complex statistical models for managing risks," he acknowledged. But financing innovations will benefit small businesses that already are strong job creators.

Lindsey said "credit scoring," a statistical procedure for evaluating default risk based on the relationship between loan performance and the specific traits of the loan and borrower, was catching on quickly among lenders.

He noted that aside from more bank financing, small businesses were benefiting from favorable treatment in equity markets. Initial public offerings, or IPOs, raised $50 billion in 1995 alone, a potent source for new capital.

Lindsey said a relatively unregulated labor market was a key benefit for small U.S. businesses. "To date government has not imposed overly burdensome mandates on employers and made the process of hiring and firing overly diffiuclt," he noted.
That gives American small businesses an advantage over European counterparts who face rigid labor market rules and it has benefited the U.S. economy, Lindsey said.

"While our private sector has been increasing employment by 1.9 million per year for a quarter of a century, the European private sector has seen barely any net job creation over the same period," Lindsey said.
